headline: Kentucky turns cloudy and colder with spotty drizzle and frost tonight; both regions become dry and seasonably cool this weekend
disclaimer: Independent amateur analysis. This is not an official forecast or warning. Follow the National Weather Service and local authorities during hazardous weather.

refresh.workflow: Update and commit forecast.json once. GitHub Actions automatically locks the prior issue in forecast-history.json. Then verify the GitHub Pages URL; every Google Sites embed reads the same file and refreshes automatically.

kentucky.name: Central Kentucky
kentucky.subtitle: Danville primary · Lexington comparison
kentucky.summary: A cold front is dropping southeast across Kentucky today beneath a compact Great Lakes upper low. Low-level saturation is shallow, so the front mainly brings an expanding stratus deck, patchy drizzle and only isolated light showers rather than meaningful rain. Northwest flow then ushers in a dry continental air mass. Surface high pressure builds overhead tonight and again Saturday night, allowing efficient radiational cooling. Frost tonight and a more widespread freeze Saturday night are the principal hazards; Sunday remains dry with modest afternoon recovery.
kentucky.currentConditions: At 7:55 AM EST, KDVK reported 50°F with a 45°F dew point, northwest wind near 6 mph, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky ahead of the incoming stratus. At 7:54 AM, KLEX reported 48°F with a 44°F dew point, calm wind, visibility above 10 miles and clear sky. An official NWS Frost Advisory includes Boyle and Fayette Counties from midnight tonight through 9:00 AM Saturday.

days.label: Friday
days.precipitation: 20–30%, mainly late morning through afternoon; trace to 0.05 inch
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS FROST ADVISORY: Boyle County is included from midnight tonight through 9:00 AM Saturday. Temperatures near 33°F will support frost, with a 40–50% chance of localized freezing conditions in rural low-lying areas. Independent analysis agrees that frost is likely and that sheltered valleys can fall below freezing.
days.forecast: Sunshine early gives way to a rapidly expanding low stratus deck as the front crosses. Shallow saturation and limited cloud ice favor patchy drizzle or isolated light showers from late morning through the afternoon, with little or no measurable accumulation. The most-likely Danville high is near 58°F before temperatures settle back through the 50s. Northwest wind runs 4–10 mph with gusts around 12–20 mph. Stratus clears from north to south tonight as high pressure arrives. Applying the established KDVK correction to the broader guidance, the most-likely Danville low is near 32°F, with colder rural hollows in the upper 20s. Several fresh models support shallow late-night saturation, so patchy valley fog is possible toward dawn, but widespread dense fog is not expected.

days.label: Saturday
days.hazard: OFFICIAL NWS FROST ADVISORY remains in effect through 9:00 AM. The official Louisville discussion then places Saturday-night freeze probability at 60–80%, although no separate Freeze Watch or Warning was active at issuance. Independent concern is widespread frost and a likely freeze Saturday night into Sunday morning.
days.forecast: Morning frost gives way to sunshine beneath building surface high pressure, but lingering cold advection keeps the most-likely Danville high near 53°F. Northwest wind stays light at 2–7 mph with occasional gusts around 8–15 mph. Clear sky, very dry air and nearly calm wind Saturday night create excellent radiational-cooling conditions. The most-likely Danville low is near 29°F after the KDVK correction; favored Bluegrass valleys can reach the middle 20s. Fresh model diagnostics also support a limited chance of shallow valley fog toward Sunday morning, but frost and freezing temperatures remain the primary concern.

days.label: Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active for Sunday at issuance. Independent concern is another round of patchy frost and localized freezing temperatures late Sunday night, especially in Bluegrass valleys; confidence is lower than for Saturday night because return southwest flow begins. A low-probability shallow-valley fog signal is also retained toward Monday morning.
days.forecast: Widespread morning frost quickly gives way to full sunshine as the surface high shifts east. Light southwest return flow allows a modest recovery, with a most-likely Danville high near 58°F. Wind stays around 2–8 mph with gusts of 8–16 mph. Sunday night remains clear and chilly; the local NWS/NBM signal is colder than the global-model grid guidance in drainage terrain, so the KDVK correction supports a most-likely low near 33°F while acknowledging some upper-30s guidance. Isolated shallow valley fog is possible toward Monday morning, but widespread dense fog is not expected.

kentucky.bottomLine: Clouds and patchy drizzle arrive with today’s cold front, but rainfall is negligible. Tonight’s official Frost Advisory is followed by an even colder Saturday night with widespread frost and a likely freeze. Saturday and Sunday are dry, sunny and seasonably cool. Most-likely bias-corrected Danville values are 58°F/32°F today, 53°F/29°F Saturday and 58°F/33°F Sunday.
kentucky.confidence: Moderate-high on today’s temperature and frontal timing; moderate on whether drizzle reaches KDVK; high on the dry weekend; high on frost tonight; high on a Saturday-night freeze; moderate on the exact Sunday-night minimum

upstate.name: Upstate South Carolina
upstate.subtitle: Clemson primary · Central/Pickens County comparison
upstate.summary: A cold front crossing the western Carolinas this morning is ending the humid pattern. Residual moisture supports brief early mist and a small late-morning shower chance, but downslope northwest flow rapidly dries and mixes the boundary layer. High pressure then settles across the Southeast for the weekend. Saturday and Sunday are sunny and cooler with very low rain chances. The main uncertainty is the magnitude of afternoon cooling: RRFS remains several degrees cooler than the official/global consensus, but clear sky and the broader independent model blend favor middle to upper 60s.
upstate.currentConditions: At 7:54 AM EST, KCEU reported 60°F with a 59°F dew point, calm wind, visibility above 10 miles and only a few clouds near 8,000 feet. At 7:55 AM, KLQK reported 60°F with a 58°F dew point, calm wind and 5-mile visibility in mist beneath scattered mid-level cloud. No official NWS point alert was active for Clemson or Central. Tempest data was not used.

days.label: Friday
days.precipitation: 5–10% through late morning, then 5% or less
days.hazard: OFFICIAL OUTLOOKS: SPC’s Marginal Risk and WPC’s excessive-rainfall areas are east of Clemson and Central. No active NWS point alert is in effect. Independent concern is limited to lingering early mist and a very brief residual shower; severe weather, flooding and threshold wind are not expected in the corridor.
days.forecast: Lingering mist dissipates quickly as the front moves east and northwest downslope flow develops. A brief shower cannot be completely ruled out through late morning, but nearly all of the remaining day is dry with partly sunny to mostly sunny sky. The most-likely high is near 75°F. Northwest wind runs 2–7 mph with gusts around 10–18 mph, then becomes light tonight. Applying the station corrections, the most-likely lows are near 48°F at Clemson and 43°F around Central/Pickens.

days.label: Saturday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active for Saturday at issuance, and SPC forecasts no severe-thunderstorm area. No threshold independent hazard is expected in the Clemson–Central corridor; the coldest sheltered pockets may see patchy frost late Saturday night.
days.forecast: High pressure brings full sunshine and much lower humidity. The official forecast, GFS, ECMWF, GEFS and NBM cluster in the middle to upper 60s, supporting a most-likely high near 68°F. RRFS remains a few degrees cooler near the lower 60s, but that solution has less independent support. Wind is light and variable, generally 0–6 mph with gusts below 12 mph. Applying the station corrections, the most-likely lows are near 42°F at Clemson and 37°F around Central/Pickens.

days.label: Sunday
days.hazard: No official NWS point alert is active for Sunday at issuance, and SPC forecasts no severe-thunderstorm area. No threshold independent hazard is expected; isolated frost is possible only in the coldest sheltered locations late Sunday night. RRFS also shows a stronger late-night valley-fog signal, but broader guidance does not, so it is retained as a lower-probability conditional risk.
days.forecast: Surface high pressure shifts slowly east while a dry northwest-flow pattern persists aloft. Sunshine dominates, with a most-likely high near 68°F. The independent global and ensemble center spans the middle to upper 60s, while RRFS is again a few degrees cooler; the broader consensus and official forecast favor the warmer outcome. Southwest wind remains light at 1–7 mph with gusts below 14 mph. Bias-corrected most-likely lows are near 42°F at Clemson and 37°F around Central/Pickens. Mostly clear conditions are favored Sunday night, although isolated fog could form in sheltered river valleys toward Monday morning if the stronger RRFS saturation signal verifies.

upstate.bottomLine: Lingering early mist and a very small residual shower chance end quickly today, followed by a dry afternoon near 75°F. Saturday and Sunday are sunny and cooler, with highs most likely near 68°F. No threshold hazard is expected in the Clemson–Central corridor. Bias-corrected most-likely lows are Clemson 48°F, 42°F and 42°F; Central/Pickens 43°F, 37°F and 37°F.
upstate.confidence: High on rapid drying today; moderate-high on today’s high; high on the dry weekend; moderate-high on weekend highs after resolving the cooler RRFS branch; moderate on the coldest sheltered nighttime readings

sourceNotes: OFFICIAL ALERT: the NWS Louisville Frost Advisory includes Boyle and Fayette Counties from midnight tonight through 9:00 AM EST Saturday. No active point alert was found for Clemson or Central at the final checks. Official alerts remain explicitly separate from official outlooks and this independent analysis.

The 11:21Z Louisville discussion expects the front and stratus to move northwest-to-southeast today, with patchy drizzle under shallow saturation. It expects clearing between roughly 8:00 PM and 2:00 AM, a 40–50% rural freeze chance tonight and a 60–80% freeze chance Saturday night. LMK explicitly favors the colder NBM solution over the warm-biased REFS branch.

The 11:30Z Greenville-Spartanburg discussion says the front ends the humid spell. A lingering shower or isolated rumble was possible mainly across the northern Upstate and western Piedmont through late morning, followed by a dry, cooler weekend. No severe-weather signal was identified for Clemson or Central.

Official outlooks are distinct from point alerts: SPC's Day 1 Marginal Risk is in the eastern Carolinas/Mid-Atlantic, outside both forecast regions, and Days 2–3 contain no local severe risk. WPC's Day 1 excessive-rainfall areas are also outside both forecast regions, with Days 2–3 focused far west.

Latest official observations showed KDVK and KLEX clear ahead of the incoming Kentucky stratus. KCEU was humid but unrestricted and KLQK reported 5-mile mist beneath scattered mid-level cloud. Tempest was excluded.

College of DuPage 13:11–13:15Z imagery showed the Kentucky frontal low-cloud and light-return band advancing from the northwest with no organized Danville radar echo. In the Southeast, the deeper convection was well east and northeast of Clemson/Central, with the Upstate on the quieter western side.

Chris Bailey’s exact November 6 Kentucky Weather Center post, ‘Tracking A Cold Front to Start the Weekend,’ and its supporting graphics were consulted as accepted source material. Bailey expects clouds and a few showers with the front today, highs in the upper 50s to low 60s before readings trend toward 50°F, lows in the low to middle 30s tonight, Saturday highs of 50–55°F, and some middle to upper 20s Sunday morning. His longer-range graphics concern next week; unreadable details and specifics outside this 72-hour window were left unknown.

Central Kentucky guidance is coherent after resolving one known warm branch: the official NWS/NBM forecast, Bailey, fresh BUFKIT, deterministic global guidance and the radiational-cooling setup support the colder weekend. The 55–60°F Friday range and 58°F center account for frontal timing, while Saturday's 50–55°F range and 53°F center reflect persistent cold advection.

The official Louisville discussion gives a 40–50% rural freeze chance tonight and 60–80% Saturday night. Most-likely Danville lows near 32°F tonight and 28–29°F Saturday night apply the established −2°F KDVK correction; the wider card ranges preserve rural-valley spread.

Fresh BUFKIT profiles and the validated GRIB package show nearly saturated shallow low levels over Central Kentucky today, with a multi-model liquid mean near 0.03 inch and an upper deterministic value near 0.06 inch. That supports drizzle or a light shower rather than meaningful rain, with a trace–0.05-inch primary range.

The GRIB fog diagnostic has 3-of-4 eligible-model support late tonight and 2-of-3 Saturday night. Because that diagnostic triggers on visibility of 3 miles or less or near-saturated light-wind conditions—not necessarily the verification threshold below 1 mile—and official forecasts emphasize frost rather than fog, it is translated to a 20% threshold-fog probability for each night rather than a dense-fog forecast.

Upstate precipitation probabilities were normalized to the post-issuance period: the organized rain had shifted east, leaving only a small residual late-morning shower chance. Drying northwest downslope flow and high pressure then support a dry weekend.

For the Upstate weekend, RRFS repeatedly forms a correlated cold branch near the lower 60s. The official point forecasts, NBM, HRRR, GFS, GEFS and ECMWF instead support the middle to upper 60s. The broader independent consensus therefore supports most-likely highs near 68°F, while the RRFS branch remains disclosed as a lower-probability scenario rather than an unresolved conflict.

RRFS also carries a stronger Clemson-area saturation and fog signal late Sunday night. Because the official forecast and broader guidance remain mostly clear, the candidate treats this as a 15% conditional sheltered-valley fog risk rather than a corridor-wide fog forecast.
